questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why twelve months fall short of a year
questions.learningObjective: compute the shortfall between twelve lunar months and one solar year
questions.stem: Twelve months measured from one new moon to the next fall short of one solar year. Using a month of about twenty-nine and a half days, roughly how short is the gap?

options.text: About eleven days, since twelve months come to roughly three hundred and fifty-four days against a year of about three hundred and sixty-five
About four days, since twelve months come to roughly three hundred and sixty-one days against a year of about three hundred and sixty-five
options.misconception: treats a lunar month as a little under thirty days, which overstates the total

options.text: About three days, since twelve months come to roughly three hundred and sixty-two days against a year of about three hundred and sixty-five
options.misconception: overstates the length of a lunar month, which brings the shortfall down to a few days

options.text: About thirty days, since twelve months come to roughly three hundred and thirty-five days against a year of about three hundred and sixty-five
options.misconception: understates the length of a lunar month, which makes the shortfall a whole month

questions.explanation: This one comparison is the whole reason the calendar has a leap month, so it is worth doing properly. A month measured from one new moon to the next averages about twenty-nine and a half days, and twelve of them come to about three hundred and fifty-four days, while the sun's own year is about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter. The difference is close to eleven days. That is not a rounding error that a table of twelve months can absorb: it is nearly a third of a month, and it accumulates in one direction only, since the lunar count is always behind. Two consequences follow immediately. A calendar built only from moons drifts through the seasons at a rate of about eleven days a year, so the same month falls in a different season every few years, and any agricultural or ritual practice tied to a season has to be rescued somehow. The calendar solves it in two ways that are worth distinguishing, because they are often run together. The solar terms are defined by the sun rather than the moon, so they stay in step with the seasons, and the lunar months are allowed to accumulate a thirteenth month at intervals so that the year as a whole stays in step too. The months drift within the year and the terms do not.
questions.hint: Multiply about twenty-nine and a half by twelve, then subtract the result from about three hundred and sixty-five.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: How the length of a lunar month is obtained
questions.learningObjective: derive the mean length of a lunation from the length of a year
questions.stem: A year contains about twelve and a third lunations rather than exactly twelve, and dividing the length of a year by that count gives the mean length of a month. What is that mean length?

options.text: About twenty-eight and a half days, since about three hundred and forty-two divided by twelve gives that figure
options.misconception: divides the length of twelve lunar months by twelve, which returns the input rather than the answer

options.text: About thirty-one days, since the moon's cycle is a little longer than the sun's year divided by twelve
options.misconception: produces a figure larger than a month can be, which the observed sequence of new moons excludes

options.text: About twenty-nine and a half days, since about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter divided by about twelve and a third is a little under thirty
About thirty and a quarter days, since about three hundred and sixty-five divided by twelve is a little over thirty
options.misconception: divides by twelve instead of by twelve and a third, which is the step the question rules out

questions.explanation: The mean lunation is a division rather than a measurement, and knowing that is what makes it checkable. A solar year runs about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days, and the moon goes round about twelve and a third times in that period, so the mean length of one lap is the year divided by that count. The answer is a little under thirty days, which is usually given as about twenty-nine and a half days and is the number every other calculation in this unit depends on. The alternatives are instructive because each one is a real error of method. Dividing by twelve instead of by twelve and a third gives a figure above thirty days, which cannot be right because successive new moons are always under thirty-one days apart. Dividing the length of twelve lunar months by twelve simply returns the input. And any figure at or above thirty-one days is excluded by the fact that the moon goes round faster than the sun's apparent yearly motion, not slower. The practical value of the mean is that it is what a calendar works with, even though no individual month is exactly that long.
questions.hint: Divide about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days by about twelve and a third rather than by twelve.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The nineteen-year cycle of months
questions.learningObjective: state how many lunar months fit into nineteen solar years
questions.stem: The calendar comes back into rough agreement with the seasons after a cycle of a little under twenty years. How many lunar months does that cycle contain?

options.text: Two hundred and twenty-eight, which is nineteen times twelve with no leap month at all
options.misconception: gives the count for nineteen ordinary years, ignoring the extra months the cycle needs

options.text: Two hundred and forty, which is nineteen times twelve plus twelve, and so includes a full extra year of months
options.misconception: adds a whole year of months, which would make the cycle far longer than nineteen years

options.text: Two hundred and twelve, which is nineteen times eleven, taking a year to be eleven months
options.misconception: uses eleven months to the year, which no account of the calendar supports

options.text: Two hundred and thirty-five, which is nineteen times twelve plus seven, and so includes seven leap months

questions.explanation: Two hundred and thirty-five months is the number that makes the cycle work, and the way to see it is to start from the shortfall. Nineteen ordinary years contain two hundred and twenty-eight months, and those two hundred and twenty-eight months come to about two hundred and thirty-four days short of nineteen solar years, which is close to seven more lunations. So the cycle adds seven leap months to two hundred and twenty-eight, giving two hundred and thirty-five. The alternative figures each represent a step that has been taken wrongly. Two hundred and twenty-eight is the count for nineteen ordinary years, which is precisely what the cycle is not. Two hundred and forty adds twelve rather than seven, which would overshoot by five months and push the seasons the wrong way. And two hundred and twelve assumes a year of eleven months, which is not a description of any calendar in use. The name for this cycle is worth knowing as well, since it is the one the Greeks worked out independently and it is still called by the man who is credited with it, so anyone reading about calendars in another language will meet the same number under a different name.
questions.hint: Nineteen years of twelve months each gives two hundred and twenty-eight, and the cycle needs a few more than that.

questions.topic: Leap months in one cycle
questions.learningObjective: compute the number of leap months in a nineteen-year cycle
questions.stem: A nineteen-year cycle contains two hundred and thirty-five lunar months, while nineteen ordinary years contain only two hundred and twenty-eight months. How many leap months does one cycle add?

options.text: Five, since the cycle's total is short of two hundred and forty by five months
options.misconception: answers a different question, about the gap to a full extra year of months

options.text: Twelve, since the difference between the cycle and an ordinary year is one year of months
options.misconception: adds a whole year of months, which overstates the correction by nearly half

options.text: Seven, since two hundred and thirty-five less two hundred and twenty-eight is seven
Nineteen, since each of the nineteen years contributes exactly one leap month
options.misconception: puts one leap month in every year, which would make the cycle far longer than needed

questions.explanation: The subtraction is short and the thinking behind it is not, so it is worth doing explicitly. Two hundred and thirty-five months are needed to keep nineteen solar years in step, and two hundred and twenty-eight months are what nineteen ordinary years would supply, so the difference of seven is the number of extra months the cycle must contain. The rate that follows is a little over two leap months every three years, since seven divided by nineteen is a shade under one extra month every three years, and that rate is the practical shape of the leap-month rule. It also explains why leap months do not arrive at a fixed interval, which surprises people who expect them every fourth year. A calendar that inserted a month at fixed intervals would drift in one direction, because the true correction is not a fixed fraction and because the number of days in a month is not fixed either. Instead the extra month is placed where the year needs it, and where that is depends on a rule about which of the two kinds of solar term a month has, which is the subject of a later item.
questions.hint: Subtract the months an ordinary nineteen years would contain from the total the cycle requires.

questions.topic: Why an eight-year cycle fails
questions.learningObjective: compute the drift of an eight-year cycle of lunar months
questions.stem: A cycle of eight years looks attractive because eight is a convenient number, but it does not keep the months in step with the seasons. How far out of step does it put them?

options.text: About eleven days, since that is the shortfall of a single year and eight years of it would be about eighty-eight days
options.misconception: adds a year's shortfall eight times, when a cycle of ninety-six months has already been counted

options.text: About three hundred and fifty-four days, since twelve lunar months are always that much short of a solar year
options.misconception: repeats the single-year shortfall as though it were the total for the cycle

options.text: About four days, since a cycle of eight years needs only a small correction once the months are counted properly
options.misconception: asserts a small error where the arithmetic gives nearly three months

options.text: About eighty-seven days, since ninety-six lunar months come to roughly twenty-eight hundred and thirty-five days against eight solar years of about twenty-nine hundred and twenty-two

questions.explanation: The point of this calculation is to see why a small, tidy cycle is not enough, and the size of the error is what makes the argument. A cycle of eight years taken as ninety-six lunar months comes to about twenty-eight hundred and thirty-five days, while eight solar years come to about twenty-nine hundred and twenty-two. The ninety-six months are short by about eighty-seven days, which is very nearly three months. So a calendar built on an eight-year cycle would put the same month in a different season every cycle, and after a second cycle it would be almost half a year out, at which point the months and the seasons have nothing to do with each other. That is why the cycle that was settled on is the awkward one of nineteen rather than one of eight, twelve or ten. The number nineteen is not tidy, and it is not supposed to be. It is simply the smallest number of years for which the total number of whole months comes close to a whole number of years, and a calendar that is going to be used for centuries cannot afford an error of three months per cycle.
questions.hint: Count ninety-six months of about twenty-nine and a half days, and compare with eight years of about three hundred and sixty-five.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: How long a month can be
questions.learningObjective: state the possible lengths of a lunar month and of a lunar year
questions.stem: A lunar month is counted from one day of the new moon to the day before the next, and a lunar year of twelve such months is never two years running the same length. Which lengths are possible?

options.text: A month of thirty or thirty-one days, and a year of three hundred and sixty or three hundred and sixty-one days
options.misconception: starts the month at a day too high, which overstates every total that follows

options.text: A month of twenty-eight or twenty-nine days, and a year of three hundred and thirty-six or three hundred and thirty-seven days
options.misconception: uses the shortest possible month throughout, which gives a year three months short

options.text: A month of twenty-nine or thirty days, and a year of three hundred and fifty-four or three hundred and fifty-five days
A month of exactly twenty-nine and a half days, and a year of exactly three hundred and fifty-four days
options.misconception: treats the mean lunation as an integer, which no calendar can use

questions.explanation: A calendar cannot use the mean lunation, because a fraction of a day is not a date, so the month is rounded to a whole number of days and the rounding goes both ways. Successive new moons are never the same distance apart: some intervals come to just over twenty-nine days and some to just over thirty, and each is counted as the whole number of days it contains. A short month is therefore twenty-nine days and a long one is thirty. Twelve months of those two lengths give a year of three hundred and fifty-four days when there are six of each, and three hundred and fifty-five when there are seven long months, since twelve long months would be three hundred and sixty days, which is more than a lunation's worth of twelve months ever comes to. The two possible year lengths are the reason the length of a Chinese year is not fixed, and they are also why dates near the end of a year are awkward to convert. A reader converting between a lunar date and a solar one has to know which kind of month and which kind of year is meant, and the calendar itself does not tell them without the surrounding context.
questions.hint: A lunation is about twenty-nine and a half days, so whole months must be either twenty-nine or thirty.

questions.topic: How long a year with a leap month is
questions.learningObjective: compute the length of a lunar year containing a leap month
questions.stem: A lunar year containing a leap month is about a month longer than an ordinary lunar year. How many days does it contain?

options.text: Three hundred and eighty-four or three hundred and eighty-five days, since the leap month is always a long one
options.misconception: assumes the extra month is always thirty days, when it can be twenty-nine

options.text: Three hundred and sixty days, since thirteen months of a little under thirty days come to exactly that figure
options.misconception: multiplies thirteen by a rounded month length, which overstates the total

options.text: Three hundred and eighty-three or three hundred and eighty-four days, since one more month of twenty-nine or thirty days is added to the year
Three hundred and fifty-four or three hundred and eighty-four days, since a leap year keeps the short total and lengthens only the other case
options.misconception: pairs a length from a year with no leap month and a length from a year with one

questions.explanation: The leap year is the ordinary year plus one month, and the month added is subject to the same rule as any other, being either twenty-nine or thirty days. An ordinary lunar year is three hundred and fifty-four or three hundred and fifty-five days, so a year with a leap month is three hundred and eighty-three or three hundred and eighty-four. The second alternative is the instructive error, since it takes the short total from an ordinary year and the long total from a leap one, which produces a year that is a day shorter than anything the calendar can generate. The third is the assumption that the extra month is always long, which is not true and which would make every leap year exactly three hundred and eighty-four days. What the two possible lengths add up to is a useful check on any conversion somebody is doing. The gap between a leap year and an ordinary one is about a month either way, and a converter that reports a gap of exactly thirty days for every leap year has silently assumed the extra month is long, which will be wrong roughly half the time. The figures also show how far the lunar year is from the solar one even when a leap month has been added, since three hundred and eighty-four days is still about eighteen days more than the sun's year.
questions.hint: Add one more month of twenty-nine or thirty days to the two possible lengths of an ordinary lunar year.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The day a lunar month begins
questions.learningObjective: state what fixes the first day of a lunar month
questions.stem: Every lunar month begins on the same kind of day, whatever the season and whatever the date in the solar calendar. What fixes that day?

options.text: The first day of a solar month, so the two calendars share their month boundaries and only the lengths differ
options.misconception: assumes the two systems share their boundaries, which is what makes a month a solar month at all

options.text: The day of the new moon as printed in an almanac, which is fixed years in advance and can be read off a table
options.misconception: treats a computed value as a pre-announced constant, when the new moon has to be observed or calculated

options.text: The day after the full moon, since that is when the moon becomes visible again and the count restarts
options.misconception: moves the starting point to the full moon, which would double the month

options.text: The day on which the moon is new in the sky, so months begin at the new moon rather than on any fixed solar date

questions.explanation: The lunar month is a cycle of the moon, so its first day is fixed by the moon and not by anything in the solar year. A month begins on the day the moon is new, meaning the day on which the moon is close to the sun in the sky and is therefore not visible, and the calendar counts from that day to the day before the next. This is why a lunar date has no fixed position in the solar calendar. A particular lunar month starts eleven days later each year until a leap month is inserted, at which point it jumps back. The third alternative is worth addressing because it reflects a real practical point: the day of the new moon has to be established, either by observation or by calculation, and different authorities using different methods have historically differed by a day, which is why the calendar had to be an official product rather than a local one. That is also the source of the distinction between a count based on the true new moon and one based on an average, a distinction which is a live issue in the twenty-first century and is the subject of a later item.
questions.hint: Ask what the moon is doing in the sky on the day a lunar month starts, and how the count relates to that.

questions.topic: Why the full moon falls near the fifteenth
questions.learningObjective: derive the date of the full moon from the length of a lunation
questions.stem: Half a lunation is about fourteen and three-quarter days, so a lunar month starting with a new moon should reach the full moon part-way through. On which day of the lunar month does the full moon fall, and why?

options.text: The fifteenth, because half a lunation is close to fifteen days and the count runs from the day of the new moon
The fourteenth, because half a lunation is nearer fourteen days than fifteen when the count starts at one
options.misconception: insists on a nearer integer for a quantity that is not close to either

options.text: The twenty-ninth, because the moon has to go all the way round to be seen full again
options.misconception: puts the full moon at the end of the cycle, when it is halfway through it

options.text: The thirtieth, because a full month of thirty days ends with the moon at its brightest
options.misconception: confuses the end of the month with the middle of the moon's cycle

questions.explanation: The full moon is halfway round the moon's cycle, and half a lunation is a little under fifteen days, so it lands on about the fifteenth day of a month that began with the new moon. The word about is doing real work in that sentence, and the alternatives show why. Half a lunation is neither fourteen days nor fifteen days; it is about fourteen and three-quarter days, and insisting on a nearer integer produces an answer that is wrong by a fraction of a day in the arithmetic and by a whole day in the calendar, since the count has to land on a date. The first day of a month is the day of the new moon and the full moon follows about fifteen days later, which is the reason the middle of the lunar month is the full moon in the vast majority of years. It is not a rule the calendar imposes, which is the important qualification: the calendar counts days from the new moon and does not adjust anything to make the full moon land on the fifteenth. In most years the arithmetic works out, and in the years when it does not the full moon falls on the fourteenth or the sixteenth, and calendars have to be dated by the moon's actual phases rather than by a tidy expectation.
questions.hint: Take half of a lunation of about twenty-nine and a half days and count from the day the month began.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Where the sixty-name cycle comes from
questions.learningObjective: derive the length of the cycle from its two counting sequences
questions.stem: Years, months, days and hours are all named by pairing one of ten heavenly stems with one of twelve earthly branches, and the pairings repeat on a cycle. How long is that cycle?

options.text: Thirty, because the smaller of the two counts doubled is the point at which the pairings line up again
options.misconception: doubles the smaller sequence alone, which is the point at which only the stems repeat

options.text: Sixty, because sixty is the smallest number that is a whole multiple of both ten and twelve
Twenty-four, because twelve pairings repeated twice cover the whole of the heavenly stems as well
options.misconception: gives a figure below the length of the stems, which cannot be a full cycle

options.text: One hundred and twenty, because ten times twelve is the number of possible pairings before any are repeated
options.misconception: counts the pairings rather than the cycle, ignoring that each one is used twice

questions.explanation: The cycle is sixty because that is the first point at which both sequences come back to where they started, and the way to see it is to ask for the smallest number divisible by both. The stems run to ten and the branches to twelve, so the pairings repeat after the least common multiple of the two, which is sixty. Sixty is not a round number chosen for convenience, and the awkwardness of it is the point. Every calendar reckoning that uses this cycle is therefore counting in sixties, which is why a name repeats every sixty years and why a name repeats every sixty days. The alternative of one hundred and twenty counts the possible ordered pairs of a stem and a branch, and it is the natural mistake to make, since ten times twelve is exactly one hundred and twenty. But each of those pairings is used twice before the cycle closes, because by the time the stems have run round twice the branches have run round ten times, and the twenty-four names of the first pass are followed by the same twenty-four in the same order. Thirty is the point at which the stems alone would repeat, which is a different cycle and not this one.
questions.hint: Ask for the smallest number that divides evenly by both ten and twelve, and test the nearby candidates.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why one hundred and twenty pairings give sixty names
questions.learningObjective: explain the halving of the possible pairings in the sixty-name cycle
questions.stem: There are one hundred and twenty possible ordered pairs of a heavenly stem and an earthly branch, yet the cycle of names has only sixty entries. What accounts for the halving?

options.text: Half the pairings are impossible, because a stem may only be paired with a branch of a matching element
options.misconception: invents a compatibility rule, since the two sequences are paired without restriction

options.text: Every pairing occurs twice, because the stems move one step for each step of the branches and each pair returns after the stems have gone round twice
Half the pairings are reserved for naming months rather than years, so the year cycle uses only one half of the possibilities
options.misconception: divides the set between uses, when the same names are used at every scale

options.text: The second half of the pairings was removed by a reform, and the cycle was shortened to sixty names to match the number of years
options.misconception: invents a reform, when the halving follows from the two step sizes

questions.explanation: The halving is arithmetic and can be watched happening. At each step of the cycle the stems advance by one and the branches advance by one, so the two sequences get out of step with each other in a fixed way. After twelve steps the branches have come back to their starting point while the stems have advanced twelve of their ten, which puts the stems two ahead of where they began. After twenty-four steps the branches have gone round twice and the stems are four ahead, and the pattern continues until the stems have advanced sixty and the branches sixty, at which moment both are back where they started. In between, the sequence has therefore produced sixty distinct names and then produced the same sixty again in the same order, so the hundred and twenty possible pairings are all used and each is used twice. Nothing forbids any pairing and nothing was removed. The practical consequence is that the names are not simply a list of a hundred and twenty things sorted, and a reader who expects to see an unused combination somewhere in the sequence will be looking for something that was never a part of the system.
questions.hint: Watch what the two sequences do after twelve steps, when the branches have completed one turn and the stems have not.

What the discrepancy does affect is the exact day of a festival that is named after a term, and it is why a careful writer says a festival falls on a term rather than treating a printed date as an absolute.

questions.explanation: The name follows from the mechanism, and the mechanism is a division of labour between two astronomical cycles. The months are lunar, because each begins at a new moon and runs to the day before the next. The year is solar, because the number of months in it is adjusted so that the year as a whole stays in step with the sun, and that adjustment is the leap month. A system with that structure is lunisolar, and the description is not a compromise but the exact statement of what it does. The commoner name, a lunar calendar, is a real misdescription and it produces two wrong expectations. questions.stem: Five solar terms are given below in the wrong order. Put them in the order in which the sun reaches them during the year.

options.text: The start of spring 立春 (lì chūn), when the sun reaches the point three hundred and fifteen degrees round its circuit
Rain water 雨水 (yǔ shuǐ), when the sun reaches the point three hundred and thirty degrees round its circuit
Awakening of insects 惊蛰 (jīng zhé), when the sun reaches the point three hundred and forty-five degrees round its circuit
The spring equinox 春分 (chūn fēn), when the sun reaches zero degrees, which is the same point as three hundred and sixty
Grain rain 谷雨 (gǔ yǔ), when the sun reaches the point fifteen degrees round its circuit

questions.explanation: The order is a matter of counting round a circle of three hundred and sixty degrees in steps of fifteen, and the five terms given are five consecutive steps. Starting at the start of spring the sun is at three hundred and fifteen degrees, and the next three terms follow at three hundred and thirty, three hundred and forty-five and then zero, which is the spring equinox and the same point written the other way round. Grain rain comes next at fifteen degrees. The rule that produces the order is the one that defines every term in the system: each is fifteen degrees further on than the last, and the whole sequence of twenty-four closes the circle exactly. That is why the terms can be given a position in the circuit at all, and why a term's place in the year is arithmetic rather than observation. The practical use of the order is in computing a calendar, since the terms are the fixed points against which the drifting lunar months are checked, and a reader working out where a month has fallen in the year needs to know the order before anything else. The one thing to hold on to is that the year does not begin with the first term in the sequence in ordinary reckoning, since the solar year is conventionally reckoned from the winter solstice, which sits at two hundred and seventy degrees and is the eighth term before the start of spring.
questions.hint: Order the terms by their position round the circle, remembering that three hundred and sixty and zero are the same point.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The steps in computing a lunisolar calendar
questions.learningObjective: order the operations that produce a year of the lunisolar calendar
questions.stem: Five operations are listed below in the wrong order. Put them in the order in which a calendar has to perform them to produce a year.

options.text: Establish the solar terms for the year, so that the fixed points of the solar year are known first
Establish the days of the new moons for the year, since the months are counted from them
Set the length of each month from one new moon to the day before the next, and number the months from the eleventh
Find the first month that contains no major solar term, and double it as a leap month
Check that the months of the year now contain every major solar term exactly once, which is what makes the year whole

questions.explanation: The order follows from the dependencies, and getting it wrong produces a year that looks finished and is not. The terms have to be established first because they are the reference the whole calculation is checked against, and they are computed from the sun's motion independently of the moon, so there is no circularity. The new moons come next, because the months are counted from them and nothing about a month can be settled until its boundaries are known. The third step turns those boundaries into a numbered sequence, and the numbering is worth noticing: months are counted from the eleventh so that the year contains the winter solstice in an ordinary month, which is the condition the later step depends on. The leap month is then inserted, and the rule is the diagnostic one: the first month that has come round with no major term in it is the month that has to be doubled, because that absence is itself the symptom of the year having fallen behind. The final check is the one that catches every error, since a correct year contains each of the twelve major terms exactly once and a year computed by a faulty rule will not, which is a cheap test for an expensive mistake.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity is the reference the others are checked against, and which step is the test of correctness.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Deriving a cycle name for a day
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for finding the cycle name of a day
questions.stem: A reader has a modern calendar date and wants the cycle name that the traditional day count gives it. Five steps are listed below. Put them in the order that works.

options.text: Take the solar year of the date, since the day count and the cycle both run on the solar year
Subtract a date whose cycle name is known from a long table, keeping the intervening days counted as an unbroken run rather than restarting each year
Reduce the number of days to a position between zero and fifty-nine, since the cycle has sixty names
Read the stem and the branch at that position, advancing each by its own step from the first name
Check the result against a table of a year or two, since a single miscounted day shifts every later name by one

questions.explanation: The day count is a continuous run, and that single fact dictates the order. Because the cycle is a unbroken sequence of names rather than a fresh count each year, the only safe way in is from a date whose name is known, and the number of days between the two dates is what has to be counted. The solar year is used to locate the dates on the calendar, but it plays no part in the count itself, which is the mistake that makes people think the day name changes on the first of January. Reducing the day count to a position between zero and fifty-nine is the step that turns a long number into a lookup, and reading the two components at that position is straightforward once the position is fixed. The final check is not optional in practice, because a day miscounted anywhere in the interval shifts every later name by one, and an error of that kind produces a plausible-looking wrong answer rather than an obvious failure. A reader who works this once with a table of a year or two learns the shape of the calculation and can then do any date in the table's range, which is why almanacs print these tables rather than expecting readers to compute them from first principles every time.
questions.hint: Ask whether the day count restarts at the new year, and what that implies about how the count must be done.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why nineteen years comes so close
questions.learningObjective: explain quantitatively why the nineteen-year cycle nearly returns the calendar to a season
questions.stem: Explain why nineteen years is a near-return rather than an exact one, giving the two lengths that are being compared and saying by how much they differ.

answer.exemplar: A good answer states the two quantities, does the arithmetic, and then draws the right conclusion about what a near-return is good enough for. The two quantities are the length of nineteen solar years and the length of two hundred and thirty-five lunar months. Nineteen solar years come to about six thousand nine hundred and forty days, and two hundred and thirty-five lunations of about twenty-nine and a half days come to about the same figure, differing by something under a tenth of a day, which is under three hours. That is why nineteen is the cycle the calendar settled on rather than one of the tidier numbers, and the reason is worth stating carefully: it is not that nineteen is special, but that it is the smallest number of years for which the total number of whole months comes close to a whole number of years. The near-return is good enough for a calendar in a particular sense. The error of under three hours is spread over nineteen years, so it is under ten minutes a year, which is a small correction to be made by the occasional leap day or by the odd month shifting by an hour. It is not good enough to be exact, and the calendar is not pretending otherwise, which is why the leap month is inserted where it is needed rather than at a fixed interval. The final and most important part of a good answer is the arithmetic check. Two hundred and thirty-five months is not a free choice: it is nineteen years of twelve months, which is two hundred and twenty-eight, plus seven, and the seven comes from the shortfall. Nineteen ordinary years are two hundred and twenty-eight months long and come to about two hundred and thirty-four days short of nineteen solar years, and seven more lunations close almost all of that gap. So the number of leap months per cycle is forced, and it works out at a rate a little over one leap month every three years, which is a rate with no tidy expression and is precisely why the leap months do not arrive at fixed intervals.

questions.explanation: The item asks for a quantitative explanation, and the mark of a good answer is that it states both lengths, gives the difference, and then says what a residual of that size does and does not permit.
questions.hint: Compare nineteen solar years with two hundred and thirty-five lunations, and reduce the difference to hours.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why the doubled month is the one without a major term
questions.learningObjective: explain the reasoning behind the leap month rule
questions.stem: Explain why the rule for choosing a leap month rests on whether a month contains a major solar term, rather than on which month of the year it happens to be.

answer.exemplar: A good answer starts from what the major terms do in the system and then explains why their absence is the right signal. The twelve major terms are the terms that begin the seasons, and they are spaced at intervals of about thirty days along the sun's circuit. There are twelve of them and twelve months, so in a well-matched year each month contains exactly one of them, and the months can be identified against the sun by that fact alone. A year that has come up short of months breaks the correspondence in a specific and diagnosable way. Thirteen new moons do not fit into one solar year, so a twelfth of the year's length has to be given up, and the month that gives it up is the one that ends up straddling two major terms and therefore contains neither of them cleanly. The absence of a major term is not a separate fact to be looked up; it is the visible symptom of the year having drifted, and the calendar responds to the symptom directly. That is why the rule is a rule at all rather than a schedule. Since the shortfall moves around from year to year, the month without a major term moves with it, and no table can say in advance which month a given year will double. A good answer then draws out the two consequences, because they are what make the rule memorable. The doubled month carries the number of the month it follows rather than a number of its own, and it is the second of two months with the same number, which is why a reader meeting an unfamiliar month name learns immediately that a leap month is in the year. And the month containing the winter solstice is protected: the solstice has to sit in an ordinary month for the year's anchor to hold, so the numbering is arranged so that the month with the solstice can never be the one doubled. The final point to make is negative and worth making, since it is the commonest error. The rule does not pick the month that is shortest, or the last month, or the one where the new moon falls latest. It picks the month that has failed to receive its share of the sun, and every other candidate answer is a guess at a pattern that does not exist.

questions.explanation: The item asks for the reasoning rather than the rule, and the mark of a good answer is that it treats the missing major term as a symptom of the year having drifted rather than as an arbitrary condition.
questions.hint: Ask how many major terms there are and how many months, and what a month with none of them must mean.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A calendar printed in one region, read in another
questions.learningObjective: assess the effect of a regional difference in the name of the calendar's new year
questions.stem: Stage one: a reader trained on one region's name for the lunar new year opens a document that uses the other region's name and a solar date the reader can check. Say what the reader can and cannot infer. Stage two: say what the writer of a document that has to cross between regions should do about it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The two dates in the document give the reader everything about the day and nothing about the name, and the difference is worth keeping exactly there. The solar date is checkable, so the reader knows the day without any help, and the lunar date is also given, so the reader can reconstruct the traditional date even if the word for the holiday is unfamiliar. What the reader cannot infer is the author's region from the name alone, and it is worth saying why rather than simply asserting it. The two words are each ordinary in the region that uses them, and a document that uses the other word is not thereby a document from that other region, because a writer may be quoting, translating, addressing an audience in the other region, or using a register that favours the other word. So the name is weak evidence about the reader and strong evidence about the audience. A second thing the reader cannot infer is that the two words name different days, which is the error the earlier gloss about them is designed to prevent: both sit on the same lunar date, and the difference is entirely lexical. Stage two. The writer who has to cross between regions has three options, and the choice depends on what the document is for. The first is to give both dates and the name, which is what the document in the item already does, and this is the safest for a document whose readers are unknown, at the cost of a little redundancy that careful readers will not mind. The second is to pick one name and state which convention it follows, which is better for a document read mainly in one region, because it avoids a form that looks inconsistent to a reader in that region. The third is to use a neutral description instead of either name, naming the day by its date and its position in the lunar year, which is the right choice for a translation or a neutral reference work and the wrong one for a document meant to feel at home anywhere. What the writer should not do is leave the name out on the assumption that it is decorative, since for a reader from the other region it is the only part of the notice that fails to be understood, and a document that is otherwise completely clear can still be rejected by somebody reading it in a different tradition.

questions.explanation: The item asks for an assessment rather than a rule, and the mark of a good answer is that it separates what the two dates establish, which is the day, from what the name suggests, which is the audience rather than the author.
questions.hint: Ask what the two dates settle and what the choice of name can and cannot be evidence for.
